sourcingNote:
This section goes further than the other culture topics: it is also about how people in the UK live, talk and behave, not only about rules.
So it has its own rule. A statement about people either rests on a statistic or an official source, or it is marked as common practice. Under each topic you find the sources and the date they are from. Where a topic has no source list, it describes common practice: it is not a survey result, and it varies by person, age and region. We write "many" or "most", never "the British are ...". More than 67 million people live in the UK, and they are all different: young and old, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, city and countryside.
Where something is disputed, both sides are shown. Rules and figures change; if in doubt, the linked source is right.

topics.title: Saying hello
topics.intro: In the UK, people often say hello with words and a smile. At work, a handshake is normal when you meet someone for the first time. Friends and family may hug, but many people do not touch when they say hello.
topics.question: How do people say hello in your country?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the place and the age of the people.
At a first meeting at work or in an interview, people usually shake hands and say: "Nice to meet you."
With colleagues you see every day, a smile and "Morning!" or "Hi" is enough. You do not shake hands every day.
Close friends and family often hug. Some people kiss on the cheek, but this is less common than in many other countries.
"How are you?" is usually a greeting, not a real question. The normal answer is short: "Fine, thanks. You?"
topics.context: If you are not sure, wait for the other person. If they put out a hand, shake it. If they smile and say hi, do the same. Nobody will mind.

quiz.prompt: You meet your new boss for the first time. What do most people do?
quiz.explain: A handshake is normal at a first meeting at work.

quiz.prompt: A colleague says "How are you?" in the corridor. What do you say?
options: I have a headache and my car is broken.
quiz.explain: "How are you?" is mostly a greeting. Keep the answer short.

quiz.prompt: Which phrase do you use when you meet someone for the first time?
quiz.explain: "See you later" and "Take care" are for saying goodbye.

topics.title: Queues and personal space
topics.intro: In the UK, people stand in a line, called a queue, at bus stops, in shops and at the post office. Jumping the queue is rude. Many people also like a little space around them, especially with people they do not know.
topics.question: Do people stand in a queue in your country? How close do people stand?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the place and the situation.
At a bus stop or in a shop, people wait in order, often without talking. The first person who arrived goes first.
On a train, most people sit in an empty seat or row first. They sit next to a stranger only when the train is full.
If you touch someone by accident, say "Sorry". Many people say it even when it was not their fault.
On the escalators of the London Underground, people stand on the right and walk on the left.
topics.context: If you are not sure where the queue starts, ask: "Are you in the queue?" That is a polite and normal question.
phrases: Is this the end of the queue?
Excuse me, can I get past?

quiz.prompt: What is a "queue"?
quiz.explain: In British English, "queue" is the word for a line of people. (US: line)

quiz.prompt: You push past someone by accident. What do you say?
quiz.explain: Many people in the UK say sorry for small things like this.

quiz.prompt: You do not know where the queue starts. What can you ask?
quiz.explain: It is a short, polite question.

quiz.prompt: On the escalator in the London Underground, where do people usually stand?
quiz.explain: People who want to walk use the left side.

topics.title: Sorry, please, thank you, cheers
topics.intro: Small polite words are everywhere in the UK, and they often mean more than they say. "Sorry" can mean "excuse me", and "cheers" can mean "thanks". If you know these words, everyday life is easier.
topics.question: Which small polite words do you use every day in your language?

table.label: Small words with more than one meaning
rows: I am sorry, or: excuse me, or: please say that again
Thanks, or: goodbye, or: the word you say when you lift your glass
Hello. The normal answer is: "Yeah, good, you?"
That's fine. Don't worry about it.
Very nice. People use it for many things, from tea to news.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. Words and habits change with the person, the age and the region.
Many people say "please" and "thank you" more often than you may expect: in shops, in cafés, and to the driver when they get off the bus.
Some people use friendly words like "love", "mate" or "duck" for strangers. Which word depends on the region. Most people mean it as friendly.
topics.context: You cannot say "thank you" too often in the UK. When in doubt, add "please" to a request and "thanks" after it.
phrases: Could I have a coffee, please?
Sorry, could you say that again?

quiz.prompt: A friend says "Cheers!" when you hold the door open. What does it mean?
quiz.explain: "Cheers" is an informal way to say thank you.

quiz.prompt: A colleague says "You alright?" when you arrive. What is it?
quiz.explain: Answer: "Yeah, good, you?"

quiz.prompt: You do not hear what someone says. What do you say?
options: Sorry, could you say that again?
quiz.answer: Sorry, could you say that again?
quiz.explain: "What?" is not rude in every situation, but it sounds sharp. Start with "Sorry".

quiz.prompt: Someone says "Sorry about that." What do you answer if it is not a problem?
quiz.explain: "No worries" means: it's fine.

topics.title: Time and being on time
topics.intro: Being on time matters in the UK for work, interviews, doctors and trains. For a party at someone's home, the rules are different: many people arrive a little after the time on the invitation.
topics.question: Is it OK to arrive late in your country? When is it not OK?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the group and the occasion.
For a job interview, a meeting or a medical appointment, arrive on time or a few minutes early.
For a party at someone's home, many people arrive 15 to 30 minutes after the time on the invitation. For a dinner for a few people, be closer to the time.
If you are going to be late, send a message. "I'm running late" is a normal and polite thing to say.
"Half seven" means 7:30, not 6:30. Say "Shall we say half seven?" if you want to agree on a time.
topics.context: If you are not sure, ask: "What time should I arrive?" It is a normal question, and the host will be happy to tell you.
phrases: Sorry I'm late. The train was delayed.
I'll be there in ten minutes.

quiz.prompt: What time is "half seven"?
quiz.explain: "Half seven" is short for "half past seven".

quiz.prompt: You have a job interview at 10:00. When do you arrive?
quiz.explain: For work and interviews, being on time is important.

quiz.prompt: You are on your way and you will be late. What do you do?
quiz.explain: A short message is polite.

quiz.prompt: A friend invites you to a party at 8:00. Which is normal for many people?
quiz.explain: At a big party, a little late is common. If you are not sure, ask.

topics.title: Paying: rounds and splitting the bill
topics.intro: In a British pub, friends often buy drinks in rounds: one person pays for everyone, and the next time someone else pays. In a restaurant, people often split the bill. Both are normal, and you can always ask.
topics.question: Who pays when friends go out in your country?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.
In a pub you go to the bar to order and pay. Nobody brings a bill to the table.
In a round, each person buys drinks for the whole group in turn. You say: "It's my round." If you leave early, buy your round first.
In a restaurant, people often split the bill equally or each pay for their own food. Ask: "Can we pay separately?" or "Shall we split it?"
Many restaurants add an optional service charge to the bill, often 10 to 12.5 %. Check the bill before you leave a tip.
topics.context: Nobody will think you are mean if you ask to pay separately. A round is about being fair over a whole evening, so do not leave before it is your turn.
phrases: It's my round. What are you having?
You can get the next one.

links.label: Culture: Tipping in the UK and the US

quiz.answer: One person buys drinks for the group, then another person does
quiz.explain: Over the evening, everyone pays about the same.

quiz.explain: Then ask what everyone wants.

quiz.explain: You order and pay at the bar, then take the drinks to your table.

topics.title: Small talk and the weather
topics.intro: Small talk is a big part of everyday life in the UK, and the weather is the favourite topic. It is not about the weather. It is a polite way to start a conversation with a neighbour, a colleague or someone in a queue.
topics.question: What do people talk about when they meet someone new in your country?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person and the situation.
Safe topics for small talk: the weather, your journey, the weekend, holidays, food, TV, sport and the town.
Many people think questions about money, age, religion or politics are too personal for a first conversation.
"What do you do?" means "What is your job?" It is a very common question.
A short answer and a question back keeps the talk going: "Not bad, thanks. How was your weekend?"
topics.context: You do not have to talk for long. A friendly comment and a smile are enough. If you want to end the talk, say: "Well, it was nice talking to you."
phrases: Well, it was nice talking to you.

quiz.prompt: Someone says "Lovely weather, isn't it?" What is the best answer?
options: I don't talk about the weather.
How much money do you earn?
quiz.explain: Agree and, if you like, add a question.

quiz.prompt: "What do you do?" means ...
quiz.explain: It is a very common question when people meet.

quiz.prompt: Which topic do many people find too personal for a first chat?
quiz.explain: Money is a private topic for many people.

quiz.prompt: How can you end a small talk politely?
options: Well, it was nice talking to you.
quiz.answer: Well, it was nice talking to you.
quiz.explain: It is friendly and clear.

topics.title: Making friends
topics.intro: Many people make friends in the UK through work, clubs, sport, a pub quiz or a neighbour. It often takes time, and it starts with small, regular meetings. A friendly invitation is the first step.
topics.question: Where do people make friends in your country?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age and the place.
Friendships often start with a shared activity: a team, a class, a choir, a book club or a walking group.
parkrun is a free, timed 5 km run or walk in parks on Saturday mornings. It started in London in 2004 and is now in many places across the UK. Many people go for the chat afterwards in a café.
"We should meet up sometime" can be a vague, friendly phrase. If you want to meet, suggest a day: "How about Saturday for a coffee?"
Many people go to the pub or a café with colleagues after work. You can say yes for just one drink.
topics.context: Be patient. A person who is friendly and says hello every week may become a real friend after a few months. Say yes when you are invited, and invite back.
phrases: Would you like to join us?
Shall we do this again next week?

quiz.prompt: A new colleague says "We should meet up sometime." What can you do?
quiz.explain: A plan with a day shows that you mean it.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a good way to meet people?
options: Join a club or a class
Ask strangers for their phone number
quiz.answer: Join a club or a class
quiz.explain: Regular meetings with the same people help.

quiz.prompt: A colleague asks "Fancy a coffee sometime?" What does it mean?
options: Would you like a coffee with me?
Do you work in a café?
quiz.answer: Would you like a coffee with me?
quiz.explain: "Fancy ...?" is an informal way to ask if you want something.

topics.title: How hiring works
topics.intro: In the UK you apply with a CV, and often with a cover letter or a short statement about why you want the job. The interview is usually friendly and focused on examples from your experience. The law protects you from discrimination, and employers must check that you have the right to work.
topics.question: How do people find jobs in your country? What do they send to the employer?
facts: In the UK, the document is called a CV (not a resume). A UK CV is usually one or two pages and normally has no photo, date of birth or marital status.
Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must not discriminate because of characteristics such as age, sex, race, disability or religion.
Before you start, an employer must check that you have the right to work in the UK, usually by looking at your passport or an online share code.
Interviews often use questions like "Tell me about a time when you worked in a team." A good answer says what the situation was, what you did and what happened.
Many employers ask for one or two references, often from a previous employer. They usually ask you first, so tell the person.
Jobs are advertised on company websites, job boards, recruitment agencies and the government's Find a job service. Some jobs are filled through contacts.

pros: A short CV is quick to read and to compare.
The law protects you from unfair treatment in the process.
Many interviews are friendly and focus on real examples.
cons: Competition for good jobs can be high.
Some employers ask for experience in the UK.
Interview questions about examples need practice in English.

topics.context: Practise your answers aloud before an interview. Use real examples with a clear start, action and result. It is normal to ask a question at the end, for example about the team.
phrases: I'm writing to apply for the position of ...
I have two years' experience in ...
Could you tell me more about the role?
Can I use you as a reference?
When can I expect to hear from you?

links.label: Culture: Notice periods and leaving a job

topics.title: Cars, driving and getting around
topics.intro: In the UK, people drive on the left, and speed limits are in miles per hour. In big cities many people use buses, trains and the Underground instead of a car. Outside cities, a car is often the easiest way to get around.
topics.question: How do people travel to work in your country? Is a car important?
facts: Traffic drives on the left in the UK. The steering wheel is on the right in most cars, and roundabouts go clockwise.
Speed limits are in mph. For a car, the national limits are 30 mph in built-up areas, 60 mph on single carriageways and 70 mph on motorways and dual carriageways, unless a sign says something else.
You can drive a car from the age of 17. You need a provisional licence, then a theory test and a practical test.
Most cars that are more than 3 years old need an MOT test every year to check that they are safe.
In London, many buses and the Underground accept contactless bank cards. London also has a congestion charge and a low-emission zone for some cars.
Train tickets can be cheaper if you buy them early or travel outside rush hour (off-peak).

prosCons.prosLabel: Why many people use a car
pros: In villages and small towns, buses can be rare.
You can carry shopping and travel when you want.
A car helps with jobs far from home.
prosCons.consLabel: Why many people use public transport
cons: In cities, parking is expensive and traffic is slow.
Some cities charge drivers to enter.
Trains and buses let you read or relax on the way.

topics.context: If you are used to driving on the right, take extra care at junctions and roundabouts for the first weeks. Look right, then left, when you cross a road as a pedestrian too.
phrases: Does this bus go to the town centre?
A day return to Manchester, please.
Is there a car park near here?
Which platform does the train leave from?

sources.label: GOV.UK: Vehicles you can drive and the age you can drive them

quiz.explain: Limits in the UK are in miles per hour.

quiz.explain: You give way to traffic coming from your right.

topics.title: Women and men at work
topics.intro: UK law says that women and men must be treated equally at work. Women work in every job, from nursing to engineering and from teaching to government. But in everyday life there are still differences, especially in pay.
topics.question: Who earns more in your country, women or men? Who looks after the children?
facts: The Equal Pay Act came in 1970. Today the Equality Act 2010 bans discrimination at work because of sex and other characteristics.
Margaret Thatcher became the first woman prime minister in 1979. There have been three women prime ministers.
In April 2024, the gender pay gap in the UK was about 13 % for all employees and about 7 % for full-time employees (median hourly pay, ONS).
Employers with 250 or more employees must publish their gender pay gap figures every year.
Mothers can take up to 52 weeks of maternity leave. Fathers and partners get 1 or 2 weeks of paternity leave. Parents can also share some leave (shared parental leave).

pros: Equal rights are in law, also for pay.
Employers must publish pay gap figures, so the numbers are public.
Many fathers take leave, and it is becoming normal.
cons: Women still earn less on average.
After a baby, many mothers work part-time and earn less over their life.
Fewer women are in the top jobs of many companies.

topics.context: In everyday life this means: a woman as a boss, doctor or police officer is normal. Asking a woman in a job interview about her plans to have children is wrong and can be unlawful.
phrases: Who is picking up the children today?
Is the pay the same for this role?

sources.label: ONS: Gender pay gap in the UK: 2024
GOV.UK: Gender pay gap reporting overview

quiz.explain: For full-time employees only, it was about 7 %.

quiz.explain: The figures are on a government website.

topics.title: Dating basics
topics.intro: Many people in the UK meet partners through friends, work, hobbies or dating apps. A first date is usually relaxed: a drink, a coffee or a walk. Everyone is free to say yes or no, and "no" is accepted.
topics.question: How do people meet partners in your country? What is a normal first date?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age and the place.
Many first dates are in a public place: a pub, a café or a short walk. People often keep the first meeting short.
There is no fixed rule about who pays. Some people split the bill, some take turns. You can say: "Shall we split it?" or "I'll get this one."
"Ghosting" means that someone stops answering and does not say why. Many people find it rude. A short, kind message is better: "I had a nice time, but I don't think we're a match."
Same-sex couples can marry in all parts of the UK: in England, Wales and Scotland since 2014, and in Northern Ireland since 2020.
topics.context: Be clear and kind. If you like someone, say so. If you do not, say it politely. A clear "no, thank you" must always be accepted. Tell a friend where you are going on a first date.
phrases: Would you like to meet for a drink?
I had a really nice time.
I'd love to see you again.
I don't think we're quite right for each other, but thanks for tonight.

topics.title: Understatement and indirect politeness
topics.intro: Many people in the UK say things in a soft, indirect way, especially at work or when they disagree. "Not bad" can mean "very good", and "I'll bear it in mind" can mean "probably not". Learning to hear the meaning behind the words saves you from many misunderstandings.
topics.question: Do people in your country say "no" directly? How do they show that they disagree?

table.label: What is said, and what it can mean
rows: I will probably not do it.
Please do it. It is a request, not a question.
It's a bit of a problem.
I think you should do this.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes a lot with the person, the age, the region, the job and the situation. Many people in the UK are very direct.
In the table the meaning depends on the tone of voice and the situation. Listen for words like "quite", "a bit", "perhaps" and "I wonder if".
A soft opening, such as "Sorry to bother you, but ...", is meant to be polite. It is not a sign that the request is not important.
If you need a clear answer, ask directly but kindly: "Just to be sure, is that a yes or a no?"
topics.context: At work, you can use the same soft style to disagree: "I see your point, but I wonder if we could ..." If you are the one who needs clarity, it is fine to ask: "Do you mean ...?"
phrases: I see your point, but I wonder if ...
With respect, I don't think that will work.
Could you possibly send it by Friday?
Just to be sure, do you mean ...?

quiz.prompt: Your colleague looks at your work and says "Not bad." What can it mean?
quiz.explain: "Not bad" is a typical understatement for "good".

quiz.prompt: Someone says "With respect, ..." in a meeting. What comes next?
quiz.explain: The polite opening makes the disagreement softer.

quiz.prompt: Your manager says "I'll bear it in mind." What does it often mean?
quiz.explain: If it matters, ask: "Is it something we can do?"

quiz.prompt: "Could you possibly send it by Friday?" is ...
options: A real question about what is possible
quiz.explain: You are expected to say yes and send it.

topics.title: Banter, irony and humour
topics.intro: Banter means friendly teasing, and it is a big part of humour in the UK. Friends and colleagues often joke about each other, use irony and make fun of themselves. If you do not know this style, a joke can sound like an insult. And sometimes it really is one.
topics.question: Do people tease each other in your country? When is a joke too much?
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the group and the situation. Not everyone enjoys banter.
Irony means saying the opposite of what you mean: "Lovely weather!" in the rain. The tone of voice shows that it is a joke.
Self-deprecating humour, where you make fun of yourself, is common. It can be a way of being modest.
If someone teases you, they often like you. A good reaction is to smile and tease back a little, or to say: "Very funny!"

At work the law looks at the effect on the person, not only at what the speaker meant. Under the Equality Act 2010, unwanted behaviour linked to, for example, race, sex, disability or religion can be harassment, even if the speaker says it was banter.

pros: It can show that you are comfortable with someone.
It makes a group feel closer.
It helps people to say things without being too serious.
prosCons.consLabel: Why others do not like it
cons: It is hard to know when a joke is meant kindly.
Some people feel hurt and say nothing.
A joke about a person's background can be offensive.

topics.context: If you are new, listen first and laugh when you are comfortable. If a joke hurts you, you can say so calmly: "I don't find that funny." If you are unsure about your own joke, leave it out.
phrases: Is that sarcasm, or do you mean it?

quiz.prompt: What is "banter"?
options: Friendly teasing between friends or colleagues
quiz.answer: Friendly teasing between friends or colleagues
quiz.explain: It should be fun for everyone, not only for one person.

quiz.prompt: It is raining and someone says "Lovely weather!" What is this?
quiz.explain: The speaker means the opposite.

quiz.prompt: A joke at work hurts you. What can you say calmly?
quiz.explain: A clear, calm sentence is fine.

quiz.prompt: What does the law at work look at when someone says "It was only banter"?
options: The effect on the person who heard it
quiz.answer: The effect on the person who heard it
quiz.explain: Under the Equality Act, unwanted behaviour can be harassment even if it was meant as a joke.
